hooks.hook: JOLTS May 2026: job openings held at 7.6M, hires at 5.2M; establishments with 1 to 9 employees showed little or no change. Market is tight but stable, small employers still hiring steadily.
In 2026 a second AI/LLM layer now sits on top of keyword-based ATS, summarizing and ranking candidates by predicted fit, not just keyword matches.
Greenhouse now runs monthly third-party bias audits via Warden AI and publishes results publicly; transparency is becoming a norm in hiring tech.
Leading B2C job copilots (Jobright, Teal) are drawing heavy billing and cancellation complaints; a trust and no-surprises angle fits B2C.
Seasonal: mid-July is the peak of the summer job-search grind and SMBs keep hiring through summer.

captions.headline: Hiring should not be the hardest part of running your business.
captions.subline: For founders doing the work between everything else.
captions.caption_linkedin:
The latest JOLTS report put job openings at 7.6 million, holding steady, and the smallest employers, those with 1 to 9 people, kept hiring at about the same pace as the month before. The market is not booming and it is not collapsing. It is steady. For a founder, steady still means you are hiring while you run sales, support, and everything else.

Here is the problem. Most small teams manage that hiring through email threads, a spreadsheet, and a few open browser tabs. Candidates fall through the cracks. Good people wait a week for a reply that never comes. The work is not hard because you are bad at it. It is hard because you are doing it in tools that were never built for it.

Hiring should not be the hardest part of running your business. A light pipeline that fits a small team can give you back the hours you are losing to admin, without turning into enterprise software you do not need.

captions.headline: Doing everything right and still getting filtered out is not your fault.
captions.subline: The system screens first. We help you get seen.
captions.caption_linkedin:
In 2026, your resume is often read twice before a person ever sees it. First a keyword parser, then a newer layer of AI that summarizes and ranks you by predicted fit. You can do everything right, tailor the resume, write the cover letter, meet the requirements, and still be filtered out before a human opens your file.

If that has happened to you, it is not your fault. You did not fail. The system screened you out, and most of the time you never find out why.

Here is what helps. Before you apply, see your resume the way the screen sees it. Match the language of the role, make your results easy to find, and remove the small formatting traps that quiet, automated readers stumble on. You still sound like you. You just make it easier for the first reader, human or not, to say yes.

captions.headline: Every applicant deserves a reply, even the ones you pass on.
captions.subline: Silence quietly costs you referrals and reputation.
captions.caption_linkedin:
Trade secret for small teams that are hiring: the rejection email is a growth tool, not a chore.

When a candidate makes it deep into your process and then hears nothing, they remember. They tell their network. In a tight market where the same people apply to several roles, your reputation as an employer travels fast.

A short, kind no does three things. It frees the candidate to move on. It keeps your name in good standing. And it often turns a rejected applicant into a future referral or even a customer.

You do not need a long note. Two sentences, sent within a week, is enough. If you are tracking candidates in one place, a quick status update takes seconds instead of getting lost in your inbox.

Try it: https://hire.risepointcareers.com/?utm_source=social&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=w29-tue-b2b

Use the words from the job description where they honestly apply. Skip text boxes, columns, and graphics that automated readers struggle with. Put your results in plain lines a scanner can read. Save the personality for the interview, where it counts.

captions.headline: You are more than the keywords on your resume.
captions.subline: The screen sorts by fit. Make yours clear.
captions.caption_linkedin:
You are more than the keywords on your resume. The trouble is that the first reader is often not a person. It is a screen that ranks you by how closely you match the role, and it cannot see the context you would explain in an interview.

That is not a reason to game the system. It is a reason to translate. Take the strengths you know you have and say them in the language the role uses. Put your results where they are easy to find. Make it simple for the software to pass you along to the human who can finally see the whole picture.

You are not a keyword. You just have to get past the part of the process that treats you like one.

captions.headline: The summer search is long. You are not behind.
captions.subline: Every application is progress, even the quiet ones.
captions.caption_linkedin:
It is the middle of July, and if you have been job hunting all summer, the quiet can start to feel personal. The unanswered applications. The roles that stay open for weeks. The friends who seem to have it figured out.

Here is the truth. A slow summer search is not a verdict on you. Hiring moves in waves, replies get delayed, and a lot of strong candidates are in exactly the same place right now, refreshing the same inboxes.

You are not behind. You are in the middle of something hard, and you are still showing up. That counts. Rest when you need to, keep your resume sharp, and remember that one yes is all it takes to change the season.
